title: A Missing Plant Is Not a Limit

scenes.tts: A coastal dune plant stops at a northern limit. Plants were established about sixty kilometres beyond that limit. Twelve to fourteen years later, that population had more than tripled. So the plant can live there. Why had it never got there?
scenes.caption: A coastal dune plant stops at a northern limit. Plants were established about 60 km beyond that limit. Twelve to fourteen years later, that population had more than tripled. So the plant can live there. Why had it never got there?
scenes.visual: Coast map with natural plants and a dashed northern limit; yellow planted dots appear about 60 km beyond it and a bar grows to more than three times.
scenes.narration: A coastal dune plant stops at a northern limit. Plants were established about 60 km beyond that limit. Twelve to fourteen years later, that population had more than tripled. So the plant can live there. Why had it never got there?

scenes.tts: The answer starts with the niche. Hutchinson gave it this form in nineteen fifty-seven. A niche is the set of conditions and resources in which a population can persist without immigrants. Temperature and soil moisture are two axes of that space. Niche space is the space of conditions. Geographic space is the map. A species can be absent from a suitable place because it has not reached it.
scenes.visual: Left: niche space with two axes and a shaded region. Right: a map where matching patches light up; one suitable patch is empty.
scenes.caption: The answer starts with the niche. Hutchinson gave it this form in 1957. A niche is the set of conditions and resources in which a population can persist without immigrants. A species can be absent from a suitable place because it has not reached it.

scenes.tts: How do we test persistence? We use lambda, the finite rate of increase. Lambda is the factor by which a population multiplies in one year. If lambda is one or more, the population replaces itself. A sink population is different. There, deaths exceed births, and immigrants keep it going. So presence on a map, by itself, does not show where the niche ends.

scenes.tts: A range edge could have three causes. Conditions beyond it could be wrong. That is an abiotic limit. Other species could be in the way. That is a biotic limit. Or the species may simply not have arrived. That is a dispersal limit. The direct test is to plant the species beyond the edge, and follow it.
scenes.visual: Map with the edge; three overlays beyond the edge in turn (conditions, other species, a stopped arrow), then planted dots appear beyond the edge.
scenes.narration: A range edge could have three causes. Conditions beyond it could be wrong. That is an abiotic limit. Other species could be in the way. That is a biotic limit. Or the species may simply not have arrived. That is a dispersal limit. The direct test is to plant the species beyond the edge, and follow it.

scenes.tts: A good test plants the same way inside the range. If the plantings inside fail too, the cause is handling or a bad year. Then cross the planting with neighbour removal. Clear half the plots, chosen at random, and leave half. Last, measure the whole life cycle. A fall in first-year growth does not show that a population cannot replace itself. Estimate lambda.

scenes.tts: Now read the result. If lambda is at least one beyond the range, with or without neighbours, the species can persist there. Dispersal is the likely limit. That is the inference drawn for the dune plant, at one site. If lambda falls below one only where neighbours remain, a biotic limit is implicated. Suppose lambda falls below one in every treatment beyond the range. If the inside controls stay at one or above, an abiotic limit is the likeliest. Keep this rule. Absence on a map, by itself, does not show where the niche ends.
scenes.visual: Three rows read the result: lambda beyond the range maps to dispersal, biotic or abiotic limit; the rule line closes.
